The rapid evolution of deep learning has generated significant ethical issues, including algorithmic bias and threats to data privacy. To address these challenges, this paper introduces a new framework for applying deep learning in a privacy-preserving manner by integrating homomorphic encryption. Our proposed solution empowers users to control the entire lifecycle of data privacy, encompassing storage, model training, and query execution. This is achieved by converting data into ciphertext, which allows for parallel computation without decrypting it, thereby ensuring that only encrypted computations occur on the server side. Consequently, the user remains the sole entity capable of accessing plaintext data, which remains secured against unauthorized decryption by the cloud service provider. To validate the efficacy of our approach, we implemented the framework using TensorFlow and tested it with the MNIST dataset. Our experiments demonstrate that our system successfully supports privacy-conscious deep learning, offering a viable pathway to mitigate current privacy vulnerabilities in the technology.

We introduce a supersymmetric framework featuring a light right-handed neutrino, which functions as a dark matter candidate. This model is a specific instance of a supersymmetric standard model extended with right-handed neutrinos, distinguished by a modified superpotential Higgs sector. Notably, the absence of doublet-triplet superheavy particles significantly reduces the number of parameters, allowing for detailed phenomenological analysis. When imposing relic density relic constraints, stable dark matter is identified as either the right-handed neutrino or a specific superpartner.

This study examines a wireless-powered communication network (WP-CN) where an intelligent reflecting surface (IRS) is employed to enhance energy harvesting (EH) and data transmission. The network comprises a power station (PS) that transmits radio-frequency (RF) signals to a set of communication users (CUs), who simultaneously harvest energy and transmit data to a power station using time-switching (TS) between transmission and energy harvesting. The primary objective is to maximize the sum rate of CUs by jointly optimizing the TS parameters and IRS reflection coefficients. To address the resulting non-convex optimization problem, the successive convex approximation method is utilized, yielding a sub-optimal yet efficient solution. Furthermore, the convergence of the proposed algorithm is demonstrated, and numerical simulations validate the effectiveness of the joint optimization strategy.

This work introduces a newly developed framework for determining the strength distribution of Gamow-Teller transitions in $^{100}$Mo, utilizing recent neutron capture cross-section data for $^{99}$Tc. Employing the formal relationship between neutron capture probabilities and decay rates within the statistical ridge method, a total experimental B(GT) sum of 2.52(16) MeV$^{-2}$ was derived. This result represents a 10% elevation compared to the previously accepted value and aligns closely with shell-model predictions. Furthermore, a revised beta-decay strength distribution for $^{100}$Mo was established, confirming that the core-core excitation hypothesis is no longer supported.

We analyze a simple framework incorporating both standard and novel fields: the former consists of right-handed neutrinos, while the latter comprises a real scalar, a real axial-vector, and a real vector field. The right-handed neutrinos drive CP violation and generate a baryon asymmetry via the mechanisms outlined. The additional fields are required to ensure gauge consistency and provide GUT-scale stability for the neutrinos, thereby enabling low-scale leptogenesis. The presence of dark matter imposes significant constraints on the model, which in turn impacts the predicted level of the baryon asymmetry. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the magnitude of the neutrino mass offers additional restrictions on the parameter space.

This work addresses the challenge of controlling unknown dynamical systems, specifically those characterized by unstable equilibrium points, missing complete system models. While previous approaches utilizing side information have demonstrated effectiveness, they depend on this data being valid and accurate. In contrast, our proposed method, a learning-based control algorithm, leverages the supplied side information to enhance performance without requiring it to be strictly true or precise. Our findings indicate that the resulting control signals exhibit lower variance and faster convergence when the side information aligns with reality. Additionally, our approach facilitates a comprehensive sensitivity analysis of stability properties by explicitly accounting for how side information diverges from the true model.

Toda conformal field theories (Toda CFTs) are integral models within 2D conformal field theory characterized by the Wess-Zumino-Witten (WZW) action associated with the affine Lie algebra of the Toda manifold. These theories are distinguished by their $GL(\mathcal{X})$ current symmetry and the existence of affine primary fields. While foundational research has largely focused on the specific case of $GL(N)$, contemporary developments have increasingly explored other types of conformal field theories. This article aims to elucidate the fundamental building blocks of Toda CFT, presenting them through an elementary and rigorous mathematical framework. The discussion centers on Toda primary fields, their fusion rules, and the Toda characterisation of the Verlinde algebra. Crucially, we demonstrate that the Toda CFT structure is most effectively constructed by extending the Toda action to a sheaf defined over the stack of Toda surfaces, thereby incorporating the $GL(\mathcal{X})$ symmetry explicitly. This extension reveals that the Toda primary fields correspond to sections of a specific line bundle within this section, while the fusion rules emerge as additive operations on sheaf cohomology groups. Furthermore, we provide a proof for Verlinde algebra, showing it aligns precisely with this sheaf-based additive cohomology addition.

Although Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are a prominent deep learning technique capable of producing high-fidelity samples from complex data distributions, training them remains notoriously difficult. This instability is particularly pronounced in high-resolution scenarios, where convergence issues frequently cause model training to fail. This paper introduces a straightforward yet effective strategy to resolve these convergence problems for GANs at resolutions of 256×256 and above by integrating a spectral normalization layer directly within the generator architecture. This technique constrains the Lipschitz constant of the generator, ensuring that the maximum norm of the weight matrix for every convolutional filter remains equal to one. We demonstrate the utility of this approach by applying it to the StyleGAN model across three datasets: CIFAR-10, FFHQ, and the LSUN Cat dataset. Results show that our modified versions achieve superior performance in both training stability and generation quality compared to standard implementations. Specifically, while maintaining the same number of neural network parameters, the proposed StyleGAN variants surpass the original in both Inception Score (IC-Score) metrics and visual quality.

We successfully implemented quantum key distribution (QKD) over a 100 km fiber optic link without using phase locking. While standard QKD protocols generally depend on precise phase locking between laser sources and long-distance optical fibers, our approach eliminates this requirement. By sending randomly modulated coherent pulses and extracting random bits from signal interference randomness, this method utilizes quantum randomness to lock the phase, thereby ensuring secure communication without external phase stabilization. This paper examines Toeplitz algebras derived from specific, frequently dense and uniformly bounded subsets within a closed invariant subspace of $L^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}^d)$ containing bounded functions that are uniformly continuous. In doing so, we demonstrate that these algebras correspond precisely to the $L^{\infty}$-algebras of uniformly bounded functions that are both Toeplitz and weakly closed. Furthermore, we establish a result indicating that every ideal within such a Toeplitz algebra decomposes into a direct sum of two simpler ideals.

Although data-centric object detection methods have recently attracted significant attention, they primarily focus on known classes and often fail to leverage the inherent knowledge of foundation models. This paper introduces **DetLLM**, a novel zero-shot detection approach designed to enhance object detection performance without prior data constraints. At its core, DetLLM employs Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate pseudo images containing drawn bounding boxes for text-defined objects. These pseudo samples are subsequently utilized to train a standard object detector. By effectively harnessing the strong semantic understanding and instruction-following capabilities of LLMs, our method achieves state-of-the-art results on the COCO dataset using an object detector trained solely on the "pascal-matches" dataset. Specifically, using a single Pascal VOC image augmented with 5000 detected boxes yields a COCO AP of **47.4**, surpassing the standard baseline of 33.3 by a significant margin. Furthermore, experiments demonstrate that our approach remains robust even when deployed in low-data regimes.

Photodissociation regions (PDRs) are defined by neutral and molecular gas illuminated by the ultraviolet radiation from massive stars. Within these areas, the gas density distribution is governed by the balance between stellar radiation pressure and gravity. This study examines the density profiles in a PDR situated within a self-gravitating cloud cloud, utilizing a two-dimensional model that incorporates the radiative transfer equation, energy conservation equations, and the hydrostatic equilibrium equation. The analysis explores how the density distribution responds to variations in external parameters, including the external gravitational field strength, external radiative field intensity, and the spectral energy distribution (SED) of the illuminating source. The findings reveal that the density profile transitions from a power-law form to an exponential form as the external gravitational potential increases. Additionally, the study investigates the specific impact of the SED on the density distribution, highlighting its significant influence on the structure of these regions. The results provide a comprehensive understanding of the physical mechanisms driving density variations in PDRs embedded in self-gravitating clouds.

Transformer models have achieved remarkable success across numerous tasks, yet the core principles behind their effectiveness remain somewhat elusive. This study introduces an innovative architecture named the Localized Transformer, which integrates essential ideas—including self-attention sparsity, convolutional feature extraction, local attention mechanisms, and positional encoding—into a unified framework. By implementing a unique type of "global" attention alongside a unique type of "local" attention, the Localized Transformer achieves competitive results across various tasks while being significantly more computationally efficient than the original Transformer. Furthermore, the model's unique ability to handle sparse data and reduce memory usage makes it particularly suitable for certain applications.

This study introduces a flexible parametric proportional hazards framework that allows key covariates to evolve over time in a nonparametric fashion. Estimation proceeds via a backfitting algorithm, and the resulting model features smooth splines to represent the covariates over time. The theoretical findings are summarized in the appendix. The approach is validated through a Monte Carlo simulation, and its practical application is demonstrated using U.S. mortality data. In this empirical analysis, variables such as age and cause of death function as time-varying risk factors that determine the hazard rate.

To reduce the computational expense of neural architecture search (NAS), recent approaches have utilized knowledge distillation to train multiple neural architecture search children concurrently. These methods function by having the children share a common architecture while maintaining distinct sets of weights and aggregating their gradient updates on shared parameters. However, we have identified that when children are trained in this manner, conflicts arise if they encounter different operators on a specific shared node, leading to detrimental interference. Specifically, our analysis demonstrates that the degree of divergence in sampled operators across the child models correlates with the level of interference they cause on shared parameters. Consequently, to mitigate these negative effects, we have introduced a novel adaptive search space architecture that varies the operator set per child model. This modification not only diminishes the frequency of conflicts but also enhances the convergence of the shared model's parameters. Empirical evaluations across various pre-trained teacher architectures reveal that our approach outperforms conventional static search spaces, achieving a consistent improvement of 0.3 to 0.5 top-1 accuracy while maintaining the same number of parameters.

Time series analysis has become increasingly vital across many fields, including economics, medicine, and engineering. Typically, analysts begin by computing summary statistics or extracting specific features to facilitate downstream modeling. This study introduces a quantum algorithm capable of calculating these features with quantum speedup for two common data formats: time series in matrix form and data on graphs. A primary innovation of this approach is its utilization of a quantum algorithm to generate the necessary feature values, a step that in classical workflows is often considered a preliminary task. By leveraging the ability of quantum computers to process superpositions of states simultaneously, this method offers exponential computational efficiency for operations involving extensive time series datasets or complex graphs representing intricate relationships. Consequently, it accelerates the initial stages of time series analysis, providing a scalable solution for handling large-scale data processing.

We define "stability at infinity" for the geometric asymptotic invariants of a topological group, then investigate when the fundamental group at infinity of a proper, cocompact, isometric acting group on a proper metric CAT(0) $\Gamma\,$, is stable. Specifically, when the Cayley-1 is proper and cocompact, and admits a proper, cocompact, and geometric finite subgroup, then the asymptotic group is stable at infinity.

Translation Quality Assessment (TQA) involves evaluating machine-generated translations to enhance translation models. This study examines the impact of translator expertise on TQA by employing a crowdsourcing methodology. We recruited a diverse cohort of participants, including native speakers, domain experts, and translators, and tasked them with translating a set of English sentences into Romanian. These translations were subsequently evaluated by other crowd members on a 1-5 scale. Our findings indicate that while TQA is feasible, its results are contingent upon the expertise of the individuals involved; specifically, ratings vary significantly depending on the demographic group assigned the evaluation role.

This study introduces a deposition matrix designed to achieve a target density profile in random-scattering systems. We validate its efficacy in two dimensions using both direct simulations and a novel random-walk deposition algorithm, demonstrating that the proposed method outperforms standard techniques by being more efficient and precise. The analysis covers the stable regime, specific to the question, and also addresses the unstable one.

Pruning techniques are essential for reducing the computational complexity of deep neural networks. However, existing pruning methods often fail to account for the heterogeneity in parameter importance across different layers and channels. Consequently, after applying these uniform pruning strategies, the resulting residual sub-networks frequently exhibit non-trivial architectures that deviate from the original structure. This study introduces a novel approach that integrates multi-level and multi-dimensional importance metrics to guide the iterative pruning of fully connected networks. Empirical evidence indicates that the surviving sub-networks generated by our method possess regular, structured forms that align closely with the original network design. Furthermore, these structured sub-networks demonstrate higher parameter utilization efficiency and achieve improved generalization performance.

This paper examines the expected value of lottery tickets, particularly focusing on the impact when the prize allows for multiple winners. We demonstrate that when multiple winners are permitted, the system's symmetry can be leveraged to efficiently compute the average value of the palps. We further show that for certain lottery configurations, the expectation of a randomly selected ticket is identical to that of a carefully selected one. Additionally, we explore the scenario involving a limited ticket pool and determine the optimal strategy for selecting a specific number of tickets to maximize expected value.

We compute the anomalous dimensions of all-dimensional operators at the six-loop order for the SU(3) non-Abelian gauge theory, focusing on legs five or more. For the case of four-legs, this reproduces results from the literature on the QCD beta function up to the corresponding loop order. For higher dimensionality, these outcomes are expressed as linear combinations of the Riemann zeta values.

We investigate how static strain influences valley dynamics in two-dimensional materials. In the absence of a magnetic field, we find that static deformation generates a dynamic valley Hall response, whereas in the presence of one, it acts as a non-linear deformation potential that can be either symmetric or antisymmetric at equivalent high-valence points. Specifically, for graphene, Tl, and MoS2, we observe that this static strain-induced effect is substantially stronger than that produced by equivalent non-uniform currents.

For the 2023 Active and Domain-Unsupervised Semantic Segmentation (ADSS-2023) challenge, we developed an unsupervised domain adaptation approach to generate pixel-wise labels for new environments. The method leverages the self-supervised technique of pseudo-labeling, utilizing an initialized teacher model to refine the quality of these labels and iteratively enhance the student model's performance. The results indicate that this approach secured the 2nd place in the ADSS-2023 evaluation. The source code for the project is publicly available at https://github.

t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) is a highly effective algorithm for high-dimensional data visualization, operating by modeling local density with Gaussian distributions and interspoint distances using a Student's t-distribution with one degree of freedom. While its success in capturing local structure is well-documented, its ability to preserve high-level, global relationships remains less understood. This study investigates t-SNE's global structure preservation by modifying its primary distribution to allow more than one degree of freedom. We demonstrate that this vertex-based approach can enhance the fidelity of global patterns, with improvements contingent on NED—neighborhood effective dimensions—and the number of free degrees available in t-SNE's distribution model. We further establish a clear link between the number NED and the dimensionality of the feature space, while also delineating the specific conditions under which this method successfully preserves global information.

This work provides a rigorous analysis of the two-dimensional Fermi polaron model, which describes a bosonic impurity interacting with a sea of fermions via an s-wave interaction. By employing a variational argument grounded in the molecular Hamiltonian concept, we demonstrate a supercritical shift from fermionic to molecular states in the ground state as coupling increases. In addition, we establish bounds for both the ground state energy and variational energy, the latter of which aligns with recent findings from quantum Monte Carlo simulations.

We introduce a digital-analog quantum computing framework for simulating lattice models of fermions and bosons using two-qubit gates. In this approach, analog interactions among $c$ qubits are supplemented by digital connectivity defined by Hamiltonian pulses. Utilizing a cost function that accounts for circuit depth and hardware constraints, we determine the optimal qubit topology, resulting in a system of spin-1/2 particles with analog coupling and restricted interaction patterns. To achieve exact bosonic and fermionic state simulations, the unfrustrated topology requires a ferromagnetic connectivity among $c$ qubits mediated by a depth of $O(c)$, whereas a circuit depth of $O(1)$ necessitates frustration in the bosonic system or antiferromagnetic interactions for the spin-1/2 representation. Consequently, we present an efficient digital analog protocol tailored to the lowest Landau level of the bosonic Hubbard model and the exact ground state of the square-lattice spin-1/2 antiferromagnet.

Counting graph colorings with specific attributes is a computationally difficult challenge. This difficulty is highlighted by the fact that calculating a graph's chromatic polynomial is #P-complete, and even more so, the specific values of this polynomial at negative integers. This complexity escalates when constraints are added to count only proper colorings that satisfy extra conditions; for instance, the longstanding open question of whether counting 3-colorings of 3-regular graphs is hard was resolved in the affirmative by a recent breakthrough. In this work, we advance this line of inquiry by establishing a specific polynomial $P_{\pi}(G)$ that encodes the count of 3-colorings for any graph $G$ meeting constraints defined by a permutation $\pi$. We demonstrate that if the parameter $\pi$ is not a power of a 3-cycle, then computing $P_{\pi}(G)$ is \#P-complete. Furthermore, we establish that this polynomial always evaluates to $(-1)^{c}$, where $c$ represents the number of connected components in a 3-regular graph $G$ that has been randomly permuted. Consequently, setting $-1$ into $P_{\pi}(G)$ yields the number of odd components, thereby proving that counting these odd components is \#P-complete.

This study explores the analytic properties of the Hitchin connection defined on the compactification of the Teichmüller bundle for a fixed genus $g$ curve. Specifically, it demonstrates that this connection remains smooth within the stable boundary of this moduli space. Additionally, it establishes that the connection exhibits polar growth at the boundaries corresponding to both the boundary and internal families arising from the stable decomposition.

The shift to remote work has become a permanent fixture in the professional landscape, presenting unique challenges for organizations to sustain employee engagement and well-being. This study examines how managers can effectively support their teams in this setting by exploring the relationship between management style, remote working conditions, and employee welfare. Drawing on data from 260 managers across the United Kingdom, the research utilizes Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to analyze these dynamics. The findings reveal a significant link between specific management styles and employee well-being, with further insights into the indirect effects of these factors through various mediating variables. Consequently, the authors offer strategic recommendations for management aimed at maximizing engagement and health among remote workers, grounded in Self-Determination Theory (SDT). These results highlight that managers must prioritize fostering autonomy, ensuring meaningful social interaction, and providing clear guidance to mitigate the risks associated with remote employment.

We present a new definition of a dichotomous matrix, extending the concept found in Loewy and Sottile (Linear Algebra and its Applications, 2010). Building on this, the paper investigates essentially Hermitian matrices that possess a specific loentent structure, as defined above. Furthermore, the study addresses the problem of maximizing the number of non-zero entries in such matrices while ensuring their eigenvalues remain within a given set of real values.

The investigation reveals a surprising connection: a bound on the number of non-zero elements in a matrix with non-negative entries and a given spectrum mirrors a known result by Fallat, O'Connell, and Thompson (SIAM J. Matrix Anal. Appl., 2019) concerning essentially non-positive matrices. This finding suggests a deeper relationship between these different matrix classes and their spectral properties.

Using the ALICE detector at the LHC, this study investigates beauty hadron decays in $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=5.02$ TeV Pb–Pb collisions, contrasting them with proton–proton data. The analysis focuses on electron spectra, the ratio of nuclear to proton collisions ($R_{\rm AA}$), elliptic flow ($v_2$), and beauty electron anisotropy. Spectra and $R_{\rm AA}$ are found to be well described by models incorporating beauty quark interactions with the quark–gluon plasma, which also account for parton energy loss and nuclear modifications to fragmentation functions. The positive $v_2$ of beauty-induced electrons indicates that beauty quarks engage with the high-density medium, a behavior consistent with predictions for light parton flow. These observations support scenarios where beauty hadrons are significantly modified within the nuclear environment, a conclusion reinforced by comparisons with $e^+e^-$ collisions at the Super Proton Synchrotron. The study concludes that the data align with models assuming the medium is only partially responsible for suppressing beauty hadron production.

This paper investigates two types of higher-dimensional geometric structures: higher-order analogues of classical matchings and new chromatic configurations. The authors introduce chromatic concepts of both Euclidean type and combinatorial kind, the latter yielding combinatorial chromaticity invariants for finite sets of color. The text establishes connections between these invariants and color symmetry patterns within the set, while outlining open problems regarding both chromatic structure types.

Categorization is a critical component of auditing workflows, prompting auditors to increasingly rely on non-explainable machine learning (ML) solutions. However, these systems often operate as "black boxes," failing to offer the interpretability required to thoroughly scrutinize classification outcomes. In response, this study introduces a new explainable categorization approach that leverages decision trees and natural language processing to automatically synthesize a rationale for each audit classification. Additionally, the method incorporates a "tree-free" classification strategy to further bolster system reliability. Empirical testing on a real-world dataset comprising 1,200 transaction documents indicates that the proposed method's explanations enable auditors to more rapidly comprehend the reasoning behind decisions and more effectively identify faulty explanations.

The STrauss process is a point process defined by a specific intensity function, where the value at point \(x\) reflects the count of other points found within a predetermined distance. Although a general method for determining the normalizing constant of the STrauss process is available, it often proves computationally prohibitive. To address this, the paper introduces a "hit-and-run" algorithm that bypasses explicit normalizing calculations. By utilizing a Metropolis-Hastings framework, this approach samples point patterns drawn from the STrauss process. Numerical examples demonstrate that this proposed approach is more efficient than standard simulation techniques relying on the normalizing constant.

The Generalized Uncertainty Principle (GUP), emerging from string theory and quantum gravity, indicates a fundamental minimum length. While previous studies have primarily examined GUP's impact on black hole evaporation by modifying the Hawking radiation temperature, this work investigates its consequences on black hole mass loss rates. Additionally, the study addresses the apparent paradox regarding the potential final remnants left after evaporation.

Scheduling problems are often complex, particularly when multiple objectives must be addressed simultaneously. Addressing multitasking in this context presents a unique challenge: tasks can be executed in parallel by different processors, yet the order of execution matters because some tasks depend on others. This paper focuses on reducing total completion time (makespan) in a preemptive environment. We examine three specific scenarios: uniprocessor and dual processor setups, each with unit task lengths, and single processors handling arbitrary task durations. For each case, we determine scheduling strategies that yield a constant approximation of the optimal solution. Our findings are grounded in a detailed analysis of the structural properties inherent in makespan minimization.

Locomotion involving legs on deformable ground is a difficult yet essential capability for legged robots, particularly when navigating uneven terrains. However, the complex interaction between the terrain and the environment introduces significant challenges that have hindered widespread adoption. This study introduces a new approach utilizing contact-rich strategies for deformable surfaces, focusing on unstructured granular ground. Our method employs a contact-rich control framework that incorporates an analytical model of terrain deformation to predict interactions and an terrain-aware cost function that integrates these estimates to optimize for safe, stable movements. Experiments using a 10-degree-of-freety robot, UNY, demonstrate the approach's efficacy across both rigid and deformable surfaces, including scenarios with unknown, variable terrain properties. The results show that this method outperforms prior art, offering superior speed and stability, especially in conditions where the terrain is both deformable and variable. The source code for this approach can be accessed at https://github.com/StanleyRobotics/DeformableLoco.

Internet of Things (IoT) networks are frequently deployed in remote and challenging environments, where over-the-air (OTA) firmware updates are essential for maintenance. However, these networks often operate under strict Quality-of-Service (QoS) constraints, making it critical to execute these updates without compromising service quality. This study introduces a novel IoT network architecture designed to facilitate seamless firmware upgrades without disrupting QoS standards. The proposed solution leverages LoRaWAN-based IoT solutions to monitor specific Operational KPIs—namely LoRaWAN uplink success rates, signal strength, and gateway connection counts—utilizing these metrics to manage data transmission loads. By analyzing these metrics, the architecture can intelligently schedule concurrent IoT traffic alongside firmware downloads, thereby optimizing QoS management during the update process. The validity of this approach was verified through a real-world proof-of-concept deployment in a hard-to-access mountainous area, where the system was tested. The results demonstrated that the architecture successfully executed over-the-air updates while maintaining robust QoS performance.

This research investigates the emergence of many-body localization within the Floquet random kicked rotor framework. By deriving a self-consistent equation for the self-energy within the multiorbiton basis, we demonstrate that the imaginary component of the local Fock space self-energy serves as a proxy for the decay rate of initially localized states. This relationship holds provided the initial state remains localized in the absence of stochastic heating. We further observe that a negative imaginary part of the self-energy signals the destruction of localization, indicating that these findings facilitate an expedited assessment of many-body localization compared to the direct calculation of Fock space transport coefficients.

Interactive graph search (IGS) involves a binary dialogue between a user and a central agent, where the objective is to identify a specific target node. This research addresses a novel IGS variant known as kBM-IGS, which is designed to locate one of a set of target nodes hidden among decoys within a bounded region of a graph. In this framework, the agent first receives an input graph $G$ and an integer $k$. Subsequently, the agent and a user take alternating turns; the agent proposes a next move, and the user validates it. The agent's goal is to determine if a valid target exists within $k$ steps of the current position. If the user can successfully navigate for more than $M$ moves without the agent pinpointing a target, the agent incurs a penalty. To resolve this, the agent must strategically interleave queries that definitively verify the presence or absence of a target within the specified $k$-distance. The primary objective is to minimize the total number of moves required to resolve this query. The study analyzes kBM-IGS across various scenarios, including specific query types, different graph architectures, and varying parameter values. Furthermore, the authors introduce a new algorithm capable of generating optimal strategies for the agent and evaluate its performance against a leading state-of-the-art approach across diverse settings.

Quantum computing holds the promise of solving specific machine learning tasks more efficiently than classical methods. However, the current absence of fully functional hardware means researchers rely on simulating quantum algorithms using classical computers. This paper demonstrates that such simulations can be conducted with limited quantum resources, specifically involving only a small number of logical qubits. By integrating a communication complexity framework with a standard reduction technique, we show that many simulation scenarios can be executed through quantum protocols featuring only low communication costs. Consequently, these highly efficient algorithms can be executed on a classical computer that simulates just the small data exchange component of the process rather than the full quantum dialogue itself. We also offer explicit implementations for specific tasks, including linear regression and kernel ridge regression, and provide detailed numerical examples. Our findings suggest that, under certain conditions, these highly efficient simulation methods could be deployed on near-term quantum hardware, thereby offering a practical benchmark to assess the genuine advantages of quantum algorithms in the coming years.

This paper examines the Steklov eigenvalues arising from Steklov Steklov eigenproblems defined on three-dimensional spaces. We derive explicit formulas that describe variations in these eigenvalues when perturbed, offering results that are sufficiently precise to identify the first non-trivial term. As an application, we establish a non-existence theorem for Steklov eigen-quantities. Furthermore, we analyze the first non-trivial term of the variation for a broad category of two-dimensional domains.

Conformance checking methods aim to align the actual behavior of a system with its specified model. While alignment-based techniques are prevalent, they typically rely on heuristics to align traces with model executions, often neglecting the inherent structural details of both the log and the model. Although recent advances in supervised machine learning have shown promise in addressing specific subtasks of alignment, they require labeled datasets that are often unavailable. This study introduces a novel approach to unsupervised machine learning for automatic alignment, eliminating the need for labeled data. By utilizing an unsupervised clustering algorithm to group trace segments based on their similarity, the method identifies alignments where deviations occur. Validated against the SMV model for vehicle speed and acceleration, the proposed technique demonstrated superior performance over current state-of-the-art methods.

Radio propagation models are essential for simulating wireless networks, estimating coverage, and optimizing network architecture. These models are generally divided into two categories: empirical and theoretical. The empirical models represent radio propagation using mathematical equations derived from experimental measurements, whereas theoretical models utilize closed-form mathematical formulas based on physical principles of radio wave propagation. This paper introduces a machine learning framework designed to develop theoretical propagation models. Specifically, it employs a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network to learn the underlying physical laws governing propagation. The study evaluates the model's performance across various scenarios, including coverage analysis and urban environments with high-rise buildings. Furthermore, the research explores how different hyperparameters and loss functions influence the model's effectiveness.

This paper introduces a straightforward and compelling semantic framework for temporal planning, which is rigorous yet permits many properties to be derived through intuitive reasoning. Based on this definition, we develop a theoretical evaluation of the dominant state-of-the-art model, PDDL 2.1 Temporal (PDDL 2.1-T). Our analysis demonstrates that although PDDL 2.1-T largely captures the straightforward paper's semantics, it suffers from specific inconsistencies. Consequently, we propose an enhanced model that rectifies these flaws, maintains backward compatibility with PDDL 2.1-T syntax, and enables the temporal planning community to adopt more robust practices.

This study introduces a power system model that utilizes the transmission network's admittance matrix alongside the concept of equivalent injection to represent load and generation. It establishes the relationships between these entities and the electrical variables they influence, specifically analyzing how model sensitivity responds to changes in the size of their respective components. Deriving formulas for these relationships, the research demonstrates that model performance is dictated by the interaction between the fluctuations in input variables and the entity sizes. Finally, it provides guidelines for modeling design, noting that load and generation entities should be placed in areas where power system equations are most sensitive to perturbations in their corresponding sizes.

This study examines a family of linear, time-inhomogeneous stochastic differential equations (SDEs) that arise from the linearization of a general stochastic representation of the Vlasov equation, incorporating boundary conditions on Poisson fields. Specifically, the SDE coefficients are derived from a linearized model of the Boltzmann equation featuring diffuse reflection boundary conditions, with applications extending to linearized transport models and, more broadly, to all linearized Vlasov equations where boundary conditions on the Poisson field are specified. The paper establishes the existence, uniqueness, and continuous dependence of these solutions on external data, demonstrating that moments of the associated solution process remain uniformly bounded in time. Furthermore, utilizing a factorization technique, the authors construct a non-local representation of the solution process, contingent upon the density of a specific nonlinear SDE. Finally, the existence and uniqueness of solutions to this nonlinear SDE are proven, provided certain technical constraints regarding particle mass and velocity distribution at boundaries are satisfied.

Software developers often articulate change requests in natural language, which creates a challenge in identifying the specific concepts and their relationships to extract meaningful concepts from these requests. The proposed solution is a new pipeline designed to derive conceptual models directly from such linguistic inputs. Distinct from existing methods, this approach does not require pre-existing knowledge bases. Instead, it leverages the semantic power of Word2Vec embeddings and the structural richness of concept networks to automatically generate high-quality, refined results. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of this methodology compared to current state-of-the-art techniques.

Colloidal gels are elastic, porous networks that can revert to a viscous liquid state when subjected to ultrasonic vibrations. This paper reports a comprehensive investigation into the rheological and microstructural characteristics of these gels under continuous ultrasonic stimulation. Using small-amplitude oscillatory shear (SAOS) and flow startup tests, we analyzed the viscoelastic transitions from the solid to liquid phase. Concurrently, we tracked changes in the gel's porous structure via small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS). Our findings reveal that, under constant ultrasonic waves, the gel behaves as a new viscoelastic material with a time-dependent response. Specifically, the storage and loss moduli decrease as the gel ages sonically, a shift mirrored by alterations in the viscoelastic behavior of the resulting porous network.

This work addresses the conjecture regarding sequences formed by repeatedly applying a specific function to the number 3, aiming to demonstrate that all such sequences eventually reach 1. Furthermore, we prove a broader version of this theorem. In related research, the author has previously proposed a novel conjecture concerning this function and provided a streamlined proof for the problem of the number 3, as detailed in arXiv:1907.01484.

Summary text generation models are essential for handling long documents, yet the quality of their outputs remains difficult to assess. Current metrics primarily focus on two aspects: the alignment between the input and output documents, and human evaluations. To address these limitations, we introduce SummScore, a novel quality metric that focuses exclusively on human-assessed dimensions of summary quality. Specifically, SummScore evaluates four key factors: document alignment, coherence, relevance, and informativeness. Our goal is to develop a more robust assessment framework that better reflects human judgment. To achieve this, SummScore leverages large language models (LLMs) trained on a new dataset consisting of 1.2 million summaries paired with human ratings and annotated justifications. Our experiments demonstrate that SummScore achieves a strong correlation with human evaluations, outperforming existing metrics that rely on language model-based approximations.

This paper addresses the challenge of reconstructing sparse signals from an underdetermined system of linear equations. We introduce a novel approach that restores just the diagonal of the cross-correlation matrix between recovered and observed data. This strategy offers a significant advantage: since the diagonal can be efficiently computed as simple element-wise products of measurement vectors, it avoids the computationally expensive matrix-matrix multiplications typical of full cross-correlation recovery. We demonstrate that, provided certain conditions are met, this diagonal cross-correlation is sufficient to guarantee the exact recovery of the original signals. Our analysis relies on the proposed conditions being easily verifiable and practically applicable. Numerical experiments confirm that our method achieves an exact recovery rate that matches the best existing techniques while significantly reducing computational costs.

This paper introduces a camera-based strategy for 3D object detection, aiming to eliminate the need for LiDAR sensors. While LiDAR is renowned for its high precision, it is vulnerable to malfunctions in adverse weather conditions, often resulting in lost detections and safety risks. Our proposed method utilizes 2D object detections from a single or a network of RGB cameras to directly infer 3D positions and orientations. The core of our approach is a learnable probabilistic model that estimates the probability distribution over 6DoF poses from image pixels. This model processes object bounding boxes through a multi-scale feature pyramid to identify features at various resolutions, enabling the detection of objects with differing real-world sizes. Additionally, our probabilistic framework facilitates the detection of multiple instances within a single image frame. Experiments conducted on the Waymo Open Dataset demonstrate that our system effectively predicts 6DoF poses for pedestrian and cyclist categories using only one camera, achieving detection accuracy that is competitive with state-of-the-art multi-camera solutions.

We investigate the statistical behavior of temperature fluctuations within an incompressible, turbulent fluid undergoing turbulence at a constant rate. Our findings indicate that the Kolmogorov length defines the transition from weak to strong in these fluctuations, with an amplitude that is independent of the temperature viscosity. In addition, we demonstrate that the temperature exhibits anomalous diffusion at large scales, characterized by a Kraichnan anomaly exponent of approximately 0.39.

This study examines the interaction between a high-energy laser and a hot fluid, accounting for the fluid's motion and heat transfer effects. The investigation begins with a comparison of the maximum transmitted and backscattered laser intensities in a stationary cold versus hot medium, followed by an analysis of the interaction dynamics under the influence of fluid motion. The results indicate that the heat transfer within the fluid significantly alters the characteristics of the propagating laser, while the fluid's motion amplifies the energy transfer from the scattered light to the fluid. Furthermore, the presence of the fluid, particularly when considering its motion, enhances the total interaction complexity. The research also explores the dependencies of the maximum intensity on the laser pulse duration, initial temperature, and velocity of the fluid.

Although modern development increasingly relies on explicit design, practitioners struggle to recall, access, and reuse these designs. Although search-based re-use of documentation offers partial mitigation, it fails to leverage the inherent structure of documentation for more efficient retrieval and transfer. This work introduces "design mining," a novel approach to identifying analogous structural patterns within software documentation. By enabling the retrieval of documentation based on source code properties, this method facilitates the reuse of design knowledge. We illustrate the viability of this approach through the implementation of a prototype system designed to navigate vast collections of documentation structures.

Processing vast volumes of streaming data is a critical challenge in contemporary data science. While stream processing microservices offer advantages such as scalability, flexibility, and real-time capabilities for handling big data streams, managing them effectively remains difficult due to their dynamic nature and the complexity of orchestrating numerous interconnected components. This paper introduces a cloud-based architecture designed to alleviate these difficulties by streamlining the deployment and operation of these microservices. The proposed framework enables stream processing to occur directly within a relational database management system (RDBMS), thereby enhancing data scalability and ensuring consistency. By leveraging the RDBMS to host stream processing microservices, the framework capitalizes on existing data and architectural investments. Empirical results indicate that this approach yields superior performance compared to traditional cloud-based solutions.

Researchers at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) have conducted searches for single production of tT particles in pp collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, utilizing datasets collected by both the CMS and ATLAS experiments. SpARQL is a textual language used to query RDF data stores. While recent Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models have shown promise in translating SPARQL from natural language without specialized pre-training, they still struggle with long sentences and produce output that lacks syntactic and semantic correctness. This study introduces a framework designed to automatically refine SPARQL generated by these NMT models using semantic verification against real-world data. Our approach employs a verifier capable of identifying syntactic and semantic errors in the translated queries and guiding the correction process. Experiments conducted on the Wikidata dataset demonstrate that this system successfully fixes an average of 78.4% of generated errors.

Academic institutions often face challenges in assessing authors and departments given the vast volume of faculty members and research outputs. To address this, we introduce a venue scoring mechanism that quantifies top-tier conference standing using citation data, while simultaneously providing metrics for venue growth and author impact. This mechanism utilizes a weighted average model that integrates citation counts across varying venues with weightings derived from citation distribution patterns. Data from the Semantic Scholar Corpus, representing leading computer science venues, confirms that this model effectively captures conference reputation. Furthermore, demonstrations of the system's utility in ranking venues, profiling institutions, and identifying specialized research areas are included. The system can be accessed at http://www.venuescore.org/.

The escalating deployment of control systems that depend on neural networks has intensified the need for rigorous methods to assess their safety. However, the non-convex nature of these networks poses a significant challenge, as most control systems are designed around convex principles, creating an inherent mismatch. This study introduces a new approach to determine local bounds for the $\mathcal{L}_\infty$ gain in networked control loops by formulating the problem as the intersection of two convex sets. To achieve this, we represent the set containing the weighted $L_2 \to \mathcal{L}_\infty$ induced norm of the closed-loop system as the intersection of several semialgebraic sets, then solve a convex optimization problem to maximize this lower bound. Finally, we validate the method's effectiveness on a practical case study involving a nonlinear quadrotor.

Furthermore, we provide a detailed analysis of the link between the graph Laplazian's eigenstructure and clustering results. Finally, we discuss the relationship between the graph Laplazian's eigenstructure and clustering results.

Tensor completion aims to recover a three-dimensional tensor from limited observed entries, a task frequently encountered in visual data recovery. Existing methods often rely on a two-stage process: first estimating a low-rank tensor and subsequently selecting its components to reconstruct the original image. However, this approach introduces errors due to the independence of these stages. To address this, we introduce a novel framework called the Hierarchical Tensor Completion (HTC) method, which simultaneously learns the tensor's rank and completes its structure. In our proposed approach, a hierarchical tensor is defined as one where each mode exhibits a nested rank structure. We formalize the completion task as an optimization problem minimizing reconstruction error on observed data, subject to achieving the minimum possible hierarchical rank. To further enhance performance, we incorporate a hierarchical patch constraint that models patches as hierarchical tensors with varying ranks. Additionally, we developed an efficient algorithm capable of handling massive data scales by leveraging the sparsity of tensor entries and patch-level constraints. Numerical results indicate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in both accuracy and computational efficiency.

This paper introduces a twisted group algebra based on a 2-cocycle derived from the conjugacy classes of a finite classical Weyl group, specifically focusing on the finite-dimensional vector space with standard inner product over $\mathbb{C}$. This construction yields an algebra, termed the Weyl group double twisted group algebra. It is shown that this structure is not just any algebra but is isomorphic to a graded dual derived from the module category of irreducible Yetter-Drinfeld modules associated with the classical Weyl group. Furthermore, by leveraging the double covering homomorphism of these groups, we establish that the Weyl group double twisted group algebra is isomorphic to the product of the Weyl group's standard twisted group algebra and specific commutative algebras. Finally, we outline a method for determining all irreducible representations of this Weyl group double twisted algebra.

Rotating systems exhibit two distinct types of anisotropic inertial wave turbulence: wave turbulence, which occurs at low amplitudes, and geostrophic turbulence, which dominates under high amplitudes. This separation is linked to the nonlinear character of the advective term in the rotating Navier-Stokes equations, which undergoes an effective transformation by the Coriolis force as the Rossby number varies. This study establishes a theoretical framework that unifies these previously separate regimes by analytically linking them through the Rossby number, thereby reconciling the distinct behaviors observed in both limits within a single model.

We introduce iterative graph normalization (IGN), a novel framework for analyzing and constructing minimal and maximal independent sets in graphs. This approach is grounded in a fixed-point iteration of a specific monotone function. Additionally, we present a normalization function that facilitates the application of IGN to arbitrary monotone functions.

This paper derives the thermodynamic characteristics of electrically tunable graphene and compares them to those of a standard two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG). We demonstrate that the gate-voltage modulated graphene's properties differ markedly from the conventional 2DEG due to the unique nature of its electronic density of states. Furthermore, we show that the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI) in electrically tunable graphene is gate voltage dependent, a characteristic absent in standard 2DEG systems.

This study investigates the nature of the radio emission detected from the exoplanet HD 207844 b. The observations, conducted using the LOFAR radio telescope, reveal a non-thermal spectrum with a spectral index of $\alpha = -1.1 \pm 0.2$ and a steep rise in flux density at low frequencies. These properties, alongside a calculated spin-down luminosity of $1.2 \times 10^{29}$ erg/s for the transiting planet, strongly indicate an origin in magnetospheric interactions. Specifically, the narrow bandwidth and steep spectrum suggest the signal arises from cyclotron maser emission generated within the magnetosphere of HD 207844 b. Notably, this represents the first detection of magnetospheric radio emission from an exoplanet orbiting a G-type star.

This paper introduces a new approach to virtually human rendering that utilizes an articulated neural representation capable of generating photorealistic images from arbitrary viewpoints in real-time. Unlike traditional methods, our framework eliminates the need for time-consuming training per character or body part and avoids reliance on specific camera constraints. Instead, we perform neural rendering directly on 3D human skeletons, learning to synthesize appearance from an implicit function of spatial coordinates defined relative to these skeletons. By employing an articulated coordinate system, we ensure smooth data interpolation across different regions of the body and handle complex occlusions between limbs. To achieve visual fidelity, we integrate multi-view images, depth maps, and body skeletons as joint inputs to the implicit function. Experimental results demonstrate that our method produces highly realistic imagery, with quantitative and qualitative evaluations confirming superior performance against current state-of-the-art techniques.

Artificial neural networks (ANNs) have recently achieved human-level performance in object recognition, yet their behavior remains largely unexamined when confronted with image challenges that impair human recognition. This study investigates the similarities and distinctions between human and ANN responses to facial stimuli across varying levels of blur, contrast, and brightness. The findings indicate that ANN performance drops significantly as these images become more difficult, mirroring a human decline in accuracy. Furthermore, ANNs demonstrate greater resilience to an individual's absence of eyes compared to humans, whereas humans appear more tolerant of missing teeth than ANNs do. Ultimately, this research highlights both commonalities and divergences in how humans and ANNs navigate visual difficulties, offering insights into the underlying mechanisms of object recognition.

This paper addresses the connection between Chern-Simons (CS) theory and Askey-Wilson (AW) algebra. The authors demonstrate that a specific subalgebra within the $(2N+1)$-th Rochelet algebra (where $2N+1$ is an odd integer) corresponds to an extension of the AW algebra. They establish that the invariants of links invariant under these AW algebra relations can be generated by Chern-Simons theory. Furthermore, the study derives a broad class of Whittaker coefficients for the central element of the characteristic representation of the AW algebra.

This study examines the thermodynamic properties of an extended Ising model featuring a distorted kagome lattice, which includes both ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic interactions. Our analysis of the ferromagnetic phase reveals a two-peak pattern in the specific heat, serving as a signature of a spin liquid state. Conversely, in the antiferromagnetic regime, the emergence of long-range order is confirmed by characteristic peaks in both specific heat and magnetic susceptibility.

Large pre-trained models like GPT-3 demonstrate impressive zero-shot capabilities, yet they remain susceptible to errors when encountering complex tasks. Previous research has shown that incorporating task-specific prompts can enhance zero-shot accuracy. This paper introduces "meta-tuning," a novel approach that goes beyond prompt engineering by providing the model with the optimal meta-structure for zero-shot learning to further boost performance. We apply this technique to a BERT-based zero-shot framework and achieve an average accuracy of 64.1% on the zero-shot evaluation of the GLUE benchmark, surpassing GPT-3 by 3.1 percentage points. Additionally, our method yields significant performance gains on specific tasks, including 1GLUE, SQuAD, and Natural Questions. Source code is available at https://github.com/ymzhang01/Meta-Tuning.

This study examines the nature of the electroweak phase transition within a scenario of strong first-order electroweak baryogenesis, a process essential for generating the cosmological matter-antimatter asymmetry. By incorporating the effects of a thermal bath and finite temperature, the authors analyze the behavior of the Higgs sector, specifically investigating the masses and decay rates of the Higgs boson and its heavier counterpart, the pseudoscalar Higgs. The research demonstrates that within a specific parameter regime, the decay of the charged Higgs can induce a first-order phase transition. Furthermore, the authors explore the implications of this mechanism for electroweak baryogenesis and the Higgs sector, highlighting its relevance to models such as the Two-Higgs Doublet Model (2HDM) and the Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (NMSSM).

We introduce an automated pipeline designed to calculate emission-line redshifts for submillimeter galaxies. This system leverages spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting to cross-match lines of sight with external catalogs, applying rigorous physical models to filter spurious matches. Additionally, the framework offers an optional validation step using a dedicated SED fitting procedure. Applied to the complete sample of galaxies from the James Webb Space Telescope's first submillimeter survey (SMASH), our method successfully secured redshifts for 100% of the 100 sources identified, with 90% of these objects reaching a success rate of 90%. The robustness of our derived redshifts is further supported by verification against independent photometric redshifts and spectroscopically confirmed redshifts from existing literature.

We investigate the quantum ground state of antiferromagnetic spins arranged on an equilateral triangular lattice with nearest-neighbor interactions. By employing a mean-field approach, we demonstrate that the theoretically $120^\circ$ ordered phase is unstable. Instead, we identify a novel quantum phase characterized by an ordered state that exhibits local spin frustration and vanishes long-range order between spins. This behavior is further supported by exact diagonalization studies of the quantum ground state of a finite quantum system.

This paper examines the confinement-deconfinement phase transition within the SU(3) Higgs framework, specifically the model featuring an adjoint complex scalar field. Using the Wilson action, we compute the Polyakov loop as the order parameter across two scenarios: the pure SU(3) gauge theory and the SU(3) gauge theory augmented by the complex scalar in the adjoint representation. By varying the number of temporal lattice sites, $N_{\tau}$, we determine how this parameter influences the nature of the transition. Our findings indicate that increasing $N_{\tau}$ drives the system toward a first-order phase transition. Additionally, we analyze how finite temperature affects this transition order.

This study employs magnetometry, neutron diffraction, and first-principles calculations to investigate the magnetic characteristics of the cubic Heusler alloy, Cr$_2$Al. The results reveal a Curie temperature of approximately 200 K and confirm a collinear antiferromagnetic ordering at room temperature. While calculations suggest a saturation magnetization of 2.5 $\mu_B$/formula unit, the experimental value is lower at 2.0 $\pm$ 0.1 $\mu_B$/f.u., attributed to the presence of non-magnetic Cr atoms and/or a partial population of their d-orbitals. Additionally, the findings indicate that Cr$_2$Al exhibits a weak ferromagnetic component of roughly 0.15 $\mu_B$/f.u., arising from a canting of its antiferromagnetic sublattices. These conclusions are corroborated by the observed neutron diffraction data.

We introduce a kinetic framework designed to model monatomic gas rarefied flows with significant thermal effects. Within this model, collision frequency is defined as the product of collision cross-section and thermal velocity, while the collisional integral incorporates the Sonine polynomial approximation at the first order. Numerical simulations of free molecular flow past a sphere and plate, as well as isothermal and adiabatic gas flows through a nozzle, are presented alongside comparisons with analytical solutions and existing literature data. Additionally, we examine the impact of varying Son polynomial approximation orders on flow model accuracy. Results indicate that utilizing the first-order model yields superior agreement with analytical benchmarks and established data compared to second-order implementations.

Semantic parsing is a crucial technology enabling voice assistants like Alexa and Google Assistant to understand natural language and execute corresponding actions. This paper introduces a new end-to-end learning approach that utilizes a large corpus of voice search queries to train a sequence-to-sequence model. This approach employs a pre-trained BERT encoder to enhance the representation of user input sentences. The study presents two primary advancements: first, a novel semantic parsing dataset derived from actual commercial voice search logs, and second, the implementation of a pre-trained BERT encoder to bolster user utterance representations. Furthermore, the paper addresses a significant limitation in current research—the scarcity of labeled training data—by introducing a data augmentation strategy based on paraphrasing techniques. This method leverages existing sentence pairs from parallel text corpora to synthesize additional voice command examples. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that the proposed approach consistently outperforms current state-of-the-art models across diverse evaluation metrics.

Precise deep inelastic scattering and proton-proton collision data are essential for a comprehensive understanding of the standard model and the exploration of new physics. Jet and heavy flavor hadron measurements specifically constrain the parton distribution function in the high-x regime and probe both the strong and electroweak sectors of the standard model. This study presents a measurement of inclusive and semi-inclusive single-tagged tag jets and transverse momentum distributions of light and semi-light hadrons. The analysis covers proton-proton collisions with a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV and a center-of-mass energy of 8 TeV, recorded by the CMS detector at the LHC during 2010 and 2011. The observed distributions are compared to next-to-leading order QCD predictions and various parton distribution function generators.

We report the discovery of Quasi-Periodic Eruptions (QPEs) in the X-ray emissions of the black hole binary 4U 1630-43, characterized by a mean recurrence interval of approximately 100 seconds. These QPEs manifest as brief, high-amplitude flux spikes superimposed on a longer-duration, lower-amplitude Quasi-Periodic Oscillation (QPO). The two phenomena exhibit opposite phase relationships, with the QPO reaching peak flux when the QPE is at its minimum. The two models proposed to explain these features are: (1) accretion onto a small black hole caused by a massive, extended accretor (a binary scenario), or (2) super-critical accretion onto a single black hole driven by a compact, steady source (a single-star scenario).

This study introduces a new non-LTE radiative transfer code designed to model atmospheres with strong magnetic fields. By extending the traditional two-stream method, we incorporate longitudinal magnetic field components into a multi-layered framework. We solve for both intensity and optical depth iteratively, utilizing the standard optical depth as a reference alongside the magnetic field as a secondary weighting factor. The algorithm accounts for anisotropic source functions derived from magnetic field orientation. We applied this model to the early-type star HD 19161, which exhibits a significant magnetic field, analyzing observations from the Hubble Space Telescope in the H$\alpha$ and H$\beta$ lines. Our synthetic spectra were compared against the star's observed spectra, and we evaluated the best-fitting model parameters. The results indicate that the magnetic field strength weakens as altitude increases, reaching approximately 1.5 kG in the stellar wind region.

It is well established that solutions to the Hermite differential equation are represented by Hermite polynomials. This paper demonstrates that a distinct set of polynomials, the so-called "Dunkl polynomials," provide solutions to a specific type of difference–differential equation known as the "Dunkl equation." Although these polynomials cannot be expressed through a generating function in a simple closed form, we derive various properties through alternative representations. Additionally, we investigate their application in constructing an orthogonal system of functions defined on the complex plane.

This study investigates the $L^2$-operator associated with the conditional expectation $P = E[\cdot| \mathcal G]$ of a random variable within a probability space, interpreting it as an operator on a space of Hilbert–Schmidt operators and analyzing its non-trivial spectral properties. Additionally, we investigate the rate of approximation of this operator $P$ using the closest Hilbert–Schmidt operators, specifically focusing on the decay of the approximation errors.

This paper addresses the development of observers for an epidemic model, specifically the SEIR framework, with the goal of estimating current infection levels. Since direct measurement of all state variables is often impractical, the challenge lies in accurately reconstructing unobserved states from limited data. To address this, we introduce a discrete-time sliding mode observer tailored to this scenario. The study examines both practical implementation and convergence guarantees, analyzing how varying sampling periods and sliding surface selections influence system performance.

Existing temporal knowledge graph embedding models have demonstrated significant potential, though they have not yet been fully optimized for downstream applications. This paper introduces a new approach that integrates temporal scopes of facts directly into the embedding model, thereby enhancing its effectiveness. Our method yields superior results compared to the state-of-the-art, achieving marked improvements in both benchmark performance and the accuracy of entity alignment tasks. The extended version with full details and experiments is available at arXiv:2302.00408.

Ultrashort pulses generated by ring resonators can achieve durations in the sub-optical cycle range, yet high-energy levels introduce significant geometric distortions that complicate the pulse dynamics. We introduce a novel ray-tracing technique specifically designed to analyze the ray geometry within the ring cavity, enabling a comprehensive mapping of all optical regimes across the resonable parameter space. This approach reveals that the pulse geometry is highly sensitive to the specific ray trajectory it follows, which is dictated by the system's global parameters. We demonstrate that the pulse duration can be significantly shortened by optimizing the cavity's global configuration. Furthermore, the study shows that the pulse spectrum can be effectively tailored by adjusting the resonator's global parameters to achieve a desired spectral profile.

Federated learning (FL) is a machine learning framework designed to train a global model across decentralized local clients while keeping sensitive data private. Despite its advantages, FL faces significant hurdles in practical settings, including communication bottlenecks, resource constraints, and the complexities of heterogeneous data and devices. These challenges often result in suboptimal global model performance and high computational costs. To address these issues, this paper introduces a new algorithm named "FedFrac," which combines fractional gradient descent with model pruning. FedFrac updates each client's local model using only fractional gradients and transmits a sparsified version of the updated weights to the server, thereby lowering both communication and computational loads. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that FedFrac converges to a stationary point with a convergence rate of $O(1/T)$, where $T$ represents the total number of communication rounds. Furthermore, extensive experiments on real-world datasets confirm that FedFrac achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods while significantly improving communication efficiency and reducing resource consumption.

This study examines a thin-film silicon solar cell integrated with a dielectric photonic band gap crystal (PBGC) behind a conventional metal back reflector. Using rigorous coupled-wave analysis, we evaluate how this cell compares to one with only a metal back reflector across varying angles of incidence and wavelengths. Results indicate that the PBGC configuration enhances absorption within the silicon layer, leading to greater photocurrent generation. Furthermore, this improvement persists even under non-normal light incidence. Consequently, incorporating the dielectric PBGC backfield is identified as a viable strategy for optimizing silicon solar cell performance.

This paper investigates the properties regarding the asymptotic behavior at infinity of iterated exponential-like holomorphic functions defined on right half-planes. By establishing a normal form for these functions, the study identifies a collection of canonical polynomials that generate them via iteration of. In the general case where functions are not necessarily real on the positive real axis, the set of such functions is uncountably uncountable. However, for functions that are real-valued on the positive real axis and possess a positive derivative, the collection is countably uncountable only.

We present new findings regarding high-dimensional expanders, a generalization of expander graphs introduced to address topological computations. This work introduces a novel family of 2-color hypergraph expanders constructed from directed graphs, addressing a gap left by a recently proposed method for undirected graphs [Lazarov and Yin, STOC 2021]. Our approach demonstrates that the specialized family from [Lazarov and Yin, STOC 2021] is merely a subset of a broader class defined by our construction. Furthermore, we establish that this wider family of 2-color expanders possesses strong properties as ordinary high-dimensional expanders.

The magnetic properties of GdInO$_3$ were investigated using AC and DC magnetization, as well as dielectric spectroscopy. The material undergoes antiferromagnetic phase transitions at $T_{N1} = 272$ K and $T_{N2} = 252$ K, a sequence consistent with prior reports. Analysis of the frequency-dependent magnetization and dielectric spectra reveals two relaxation times, $\tau_1$ and $\tau_2$, which exhibit a temperature dependence well-described by the double Arrhenius law.

Graph embeddings serve as a powerful tool for analyzing complex networks by condensing their structure and semantics into low-dimensional representations. While current methods predominantly target general graphs, real-world applications frequently involve specific patterns characterized by varying densities and connectivity levels. To address this, we introduce Sparse Structured Network Embedding (SSNE), a novel approach designed to capture the topology of general sparse networks. By integrating a latent space model with a Bayesian framework, SSNE effectively handles sparse edges and underpins a new class of probabilistic models for sparse data. This method enables the integration of multiple network data sources by leveraging their shared latent space, thereby facilitating the inference of unobserved links. Empirical evaluations on both simulated datasets and real-world applications confirm that SSNE outperforms existing techniques in accuracy.

A jet-of-atoms technique employing a water jet fabricates extensive etched regions within glass enclosures. This approach successfully etches areas reaching up to 10 cm in length, with performance validated through atomic spectroscopy. Specifically, etched zones of 30 cm enable the construction of compact, cost-effective, and durable vapor cells suitable for applications such as laser spectroscopy.

This paper introduces a novel, high-performance model designed to minimize the gap between the achieved capacity and the Shannon limit for any given 3D format. The approach employs a three-layer architecture that accounts for cross-layer interactions and incorporates the concept of "cross-layer diversity." Simulations indicate that the proposed method achieves an average efficiency improvement of 0.1 dB over the benchmark model (MIM), resulting in dual-polarization 4D formats that are 0.1 dB closer to the Shannon limit. Additionally, the model demonstrates robust performance across various dual-polarization 4D configurations.

Detecting wildfires early is crucial for mitigating risks to life, property, and the environment. This study introduces a novel deep learning model for identifying wildfires in satellite imagery, leveraging the efficiency of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and the precision of attention mechanisms. By integrating a parallel attention structure with two distinct attention blocks, the network enhances the ability to distinguish wildfire regions. Additionally, the implementation of a feature pyramid network (FPN) ensures the system effectively captures both fine details and expansive contextual information. Experimental evaluations on the FIRMS dataset demonstrate that this approach surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods, achieving a mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) of 80.20%. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Anubhav-2000/FIRE-Detection.

This paper introduces an innovative depression detection dataset derived from Twitter content, categorized into three severity levels: mild, moderate, and severe. The dataset comprises 1,000 manually annotated samples for each category. To facilitate this labeling process, two leading language models—BERT and RoBERTa—were employed to automatically identify and retrieve depression-related posts from the source material. Subsequently, these models were fine-tuned to generate labels indicating the specific type of depression exhibited by each user. Our findings demonstrate that the annotation quality achieved through fine-tuning these models is superior to that of human annotators. Furthermore, we evaluated the proposed dataset and annotation strategy by training various depression detection models, with BERT achieving the highest accuracy, surpassing RoBERTa by a margin of 2.4%.

This study employs a System of Systems (SIS) model to analyze the impact of the Coronavirus pandemic.
